questions.question_stem: An analyst applies day 6's co-spend rule to a transaction with 50 inputs from separate users. What goes wrong?
questions.correct_answer: Unrelated owners merge into one cluster and later hops inherit the error, so the transaction should be marked a CoinJoin.
incorrect_answers: The 50 inputs become one confirmed owner, so later hops are traced with higher confidence than a normal co-spend.
The rule fails safely, because a transaction with that many inputs is ignored by any clustering method in use.
The cluster splits into 50 clusters, because the rule treats each input as its own owner when there are many.
questions.explanation: A CoinJoin is many owners in one transaction. Treating its inputs as one wallet makes clustering 'erroneously merge unrelated address groups'; the move is to mark it and not cluster across it.

questions.question_stem: A Whirlpool round has five inputs and five equal outputs, and one input is in a ransom cluster. What can the analyst say?
questions.correct_answer: Any of the five outputs could be the ransom's; the anonymity set is five and nothing picks one.
incorrect_answers: The output at the same position as the ransom input is the ransom's, because positions are kept.
Four are ruled out because an output must differ from the others to be the ransom's, leaving just one.
All five are the ransom's, because every output of a CoinJoin inherits the cluster of all the inputs.
questions.explanation: Equal outputs are the design. The anonymity set is the outputs a coin could have become; the larger it is, the weaker any guess. Which one is undetermined.

specific_source.anchor: A CoinJoin is many owners in one transaction

questions.question_stem: The lesson says spotting a CoinJoin is easy but seeing through one is not. Why?
questions.correct_answer: Equal outputs are the design and show on the chain; which output belongs to which input is what the design hides.
incorrect_answers: Researchers can detect only some wallets' CoinJoins, so most still look like ordinary payments on the chain.
The coordinator publishes the equal outputs but encrypts the inputs, so only the inputs stay hidden to the analyst.
A CoinJoin moves the coins to a different ledger from the cluster's, so the trace changes chains at the mix point.
questions.explanation: Stütz et al. detected Wasabi 1.x and Samourai CoinJoins with over 99% accuracy. Recognition is easy because the shape is the mixing; the input-to-output link stays undetermined.

questions.question_stem: Wasabi 1.x rounds paid out about 0.1 BTC outputs of one size. What changed in Wasabi 2.x for an analyst looking for the sign?
questions.correct_answer: WabiSabi allows arbitrary denominations, so the single-denomination sign of Wasabi 1.x no longer applies.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because Wasabi 2.x rounds still pay out outputs of one fixed size, so the sign is the same as before.
Wasabi 2.x moved to fixed pool sizes of 0.001, 0.01, 0.05 and 0.5 BTC, as Whirlpool had before it.
Wasabi 2.x rounds hide the outputs from the chain, so there is no sign left that an analyst can check.
questions.explanation: Wasabi 1.x used one denomination near 0.1 BTC, Whirlpool used fixed pool sizes, and WabiSabi allows arbitrary denominations. The analyst must know which design is in play.

questions.question_stem: Two outputs of the same Whirlpool round are later spent together in one transaction. What does that do to the mix?
questions.correct_answer: The co-spend rule links the two outputs to one owner again, which is one strong line, so the lead is Moderate.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because outputs that left a CoinJoin can no longer be linked by anything left on the chain.
It proves both outputs belong to the ransom cluster, because the co-spend rule is certain, so it is High.
It is Low, because any transaction that touches a mixed output is a matter of timing and nothing more.
questions.explanation: The mix is one transaction and users' habits surround it. A post-mix co-spend undoes the mix by the co-spend rule; one strong line is Moderate on the course scale.

questions.question_stem: Three outputs of a CoinJoin reach one exchange deposit address ten blocks later. How should the note rate and word this?
questions.correct_answer: A lead only, Low: timing alone is behavior, so it names something to ask about and is not a finding.
incorrect_answers: Moderate, because three outputs landing together is a co-spend of the ransom cluster's own coins at once.
High, because the exchange deposit is a service and a service always supplies an independent line.
No lead at all, because a CoinJoin makes every later link impossible for an analyst to state.
questions.explanation: Timing alone is Low on the course scale. The exchange may hold records that could become a second, independent line, but until then the deposit is a lead for an agent.

questions.question_stem: What is the key difference between a mixer and a CoinJoin for the analyst?
questions.correct_answer: A mixer pools deposits and pays out other coins, so each withdrawal is a new start; a CoinJoin is one transaction.
incorrect_answers: A mixer builds one transaction that every user signs, while a CoinJoin keeps the coins you were following all along.
A mixer returns the same coins to a new address, while a CoinJoin pays out the coins of the other users in its round.
A mixer is always a smart contract on Ethereum, while a CoinJoin is always a service with a custodian who holds the coins.
questions.explanation: In a mixer the coins out are not the coins in, so the trace ends at the deposit. The note labels the mixer, with date and amount, and treats each withdrawal as a new start.

questions.question_stem: How does Tornado Cash differ in kind from a Bitcoin mixer such as Bitcoin Fog?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin Fog was a custodial service with an operator, while Tornado Cash is a set of contracts on Ethereum.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin Fog was a contract anyone could call, while Tornado Cash was a hosted service with a single operator.
Both pooled coins on Ethereum, but Bitcoin Fog paid out the same coins and Tornado Cash paid out others.
Both are CoinJoins, but Bitcoin Fog used equal outputs and Tornado Cash used arbitrary denominations.
questions.explanation: The slide contrasts custodial services on Bitcoin (Bitcoin Fog, Sinbad) with a contract on Ethereum. FinCEN calls such a provider a money transmitter; Tornado Cash's sanctions are covered in day 5 ②.

questions.question_stem: Researchers cut Tornado Cash anonymity sets by an average of about a quarter. What does the lesson say made that possible?
questions.correct_answer: Users' own habits, such as reusing an address or linking deposit and withdrawal addresses, not a flaw in the protocol.
incorrect_answers: They broke the pool's cryptography, so any deposit can be matched to its withdrawal whenever they wish to do so.
The pool is weak because Ethereum has no addresses, so any withdrawal links straight back to its own deposit.
The pool's coordinator kept logs of its users, which the researchers then read to shrink the sets of possible users.
questions.explanation: Wang et al. cut Tornado Cash anonymity sets by an average of 27.34% on Ethereum using heuristics built on users' mistakes. Every row of the table is a habit, not a protocol flaw.

questions.question_stem: A Tornado Cash withdrawal address is also the address that made the deposit. How does the lesson rate that link?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate: using one address on both sides is a user mistake that ties the withdrawal back to the deposit.
incorrect_answers: High: a single address on both sides is proof of ownership, since only one party can sign for that address.
Low: address reuse is only a matter of timing and shows nothing at all about who owns the address.
Undetermined: a mixer breaks every link, so even a reused address says nothing about the pool at all.
questions.explanation: The lesson's table rates 'same address both sides' Moderate, and 'matching amounts' and 'timing' Low. These are users' mistakes, not protocol flaws.

questions.question_stem: An ordinary-looking payment has two inputs, a payment output and change. Why can the analyst not rule out a PayJoin?
questions.correct_answer: A PayJoin looks like a normal payment with no equal outputs, so a co-spend there stays Moderate, never High.
incorrect_answers: PayJoins always show equal outputs, so their absence now rules one out and the co-spend can safely be rated as High.
PayJoin makes the sender's inputs unspendable, so a payment with two inputs cannot come from the sender at all.
A PayJoin needs three parties to sign, so a two-party payment is never one and the co-spend rule is safe to use.
questions.explanation: In a PayJoin sender and receiver both add inputs. BIP 78 says the common-input heuristic 'becomes unreliable', with no warning sign, which is why the co-spend row stops at Moderate.

questions.question_stem: An address in the trace received a tiny payment from a sanctioned address. What can the analyst say?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing about a link: anyone can pay any address, so a dust payment says nothing about its sender.
incorrect_answers: The address is exposed to the sanctioned owner, so the note should list it as a related party.
The address belongs to the sanctioned owner, since small payments go only between a person's own addresses.
The two addresses form one cluster, since a payment between two addresses counts as a co-spend.
questions.explanation: Dust is bait: a tiny payment is sent hoping the wallet spends it with the owner's other coins. If the owner does, the co-spend is about the owner's coins, not the duster's.

questions.question_stem: A transaction has the Whirlpool shape and is dated 2025. How should the note describe who ran it and what it shows?
questions.correct_answer: Not Samourai's, which was shut down in April 2024; date the coordinator, and a CoinJoin alone is not evidence of a crime.
incorrect_answers: Samourai's, because Whirlpool shapes can only be produced by that coordinator, so the user was one of its customers.
Unknown and unimportant, because the coordinator never affects the trace and so the date is not needed in the note.
The user's own, because Whirlpool rounds are built by the user's wallet and need no coordinator at all to run.
questions.explanation: The operators ended; the technique did not. A new Whirlpool coordinator started on 31 May 2025, and CoinJoins 'are used by both lawful and unlawful actors'. Date every coordinator claim.

questions.question_stem: In the lesson's limits-of-tracing note, a CoinJoin step has 50 outputs and five are the ransom's. How is that step written?
questions.correct_answer: As a stop: the anonymity set is 50 and which five are the ransom's is undetermined.
incorrect_answers: As a guess: the student picks five of the outputs and rates them Low to keep tracing.
As a link: the five ransom outputs are named by position, and the step is rated Moderate.
As an error: a CoinJoin step never goes in the note, since only services get a rating.
questions.explanation: The note says where the trace stops, why, what still shows and how sure. Undetermined is an answer, and the leads after the stop each carry their own confidence word.

questions.question_stem: Transaction A has 300 outputs in several amounts, each repeated many times. Transaction B has five inputs and five outputs, all 0.01 BTC. Which reading fits the assigned reading's designs?
questions.correct_answer: A fits a Wasabi 2.x round, where wallets pick their own amounts; B fits a Whirlpool pool round.
incorrect_answers: A is not a CoinJoin, because its output amounts are not all equal; B fits a Whirlpool pool round.
A fits a Whirlpool TX0 split into pool sizes; B fits a Wasabi 1.x round of one fixed size.
A fits a Wasabi 1.x round, where wallets pick their own amounts; B fits a Wasabi 2.x round.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading describes Wasabi 2.x (WabiSabi) as allowing arbitrary output amounts chosen by each wallet, in rounds of low hundreds of inputs and outputs, so many repeated values among hundreds of outputs fit it. Whirlpool rounds are small (5 by 5, later up to 8 by 8) with every output at the pool's fixed size. Different amounts do not rule out a CoinJoin.

questions.question_stem: A ransom cluster pays one transaction with one input, several outputs just above 0.05 BTC and a change output. What is it, and what does it do to the trace?
questions.correct_answer: A Whirlpool TX0 pre-mix split; its outputs are still the cluster's, so the trace continues.
incorrect_answers: A Whirlpool CoinJoin round; its outputs belong to several owners, so the trace stops here.
A coordinator payout of mixed coins; its outputs are other users' money, so the trace is lost.
A post-mix spend by the wallet; its outputs have already left the mix, so the trace resumes.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading says Whirlpool first splits any fresh input into outputs of the pool's size in a TX0 transaction, which also pays the coordinator's fee and leaves a change output that is not mixed. TX0 has one owner, so it is still the cluster's own spend; the trace stops only at the CoinJoin rounds that follow.

questions.question_stem: The inputs of a CoinJoin are spent in one transaction. Why, per the reading's protocol steps, do they not share an owner?
questions.correct_answer: Each wallet registers and signs only its own inputs; the coordinator only gathers them into one.
incorrect_answers: The coordinator signs every input with its own key, so they only look as if one owner spent them.
The coordinator takes custody of each input first, then pays new coins from its pool to users.
Each input is first spent in its own transaction, and the coordinator later bundles them in one block.
questions.explanation: In the assigned reading's protocol steps, each wallet registers its own inputs and proves it owns them, registers its own new outputs, checks the final transaction and signs only its own inputs; the coordinator collects the signatures and broadcasts. The coordinator never holds the coins, which is what separates these designs from a custodial mixer. Inputs signed by several wallets are several owners, so the co-spend rule does not apply.
questions.lesson_block: A CoinJoin is many owners in one transaction

questions.question_stem: A colleague says the 2024 coordinator shutdowns ended Bitcoin CoinJoin. What does the assigned reading show, as of its November 2025 data?
questions.correct_answer: Wasabi 2.x mixing moved to new coordinators and passed its pre-shutdown level, mostly through one.
incorrect_answers: CoinJoin mixing fell to a small share of its old level, since no major coordinator was left running.
Wasabi 2.x mixing spread evenly across many new coordinators, so none holds most of the volume.
Whirlpool came back under a new coordinator and now carries most of the mixed volume on Bitcoin.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading finds that after the 2024 shutdowns new Wasabi 2.x coordinators took over, and one of them, kruw.io, carries over 99% of mixed liquidity and has passed the pre-shutdown level (as of 10 Nov 2025). A new Whirlpool coordinator started in May 2025 but has little activity. The operators stopped; the technique did not.
